<reason>PRO built a clear decision rule (bounded, relocating dollars vs. compounding strategic delay) and then kept narrowing the debate onto CON's weakest joints: CON's own "slower at first" concession, the "budget line" vs. "national emergency" tension, and the unshown "durable hit" to toolmakers with record order books. PRO's A1 was notably honest ("None") and then reframed persuasively: the motion is about development, fielded systems are already-trained frontier runs, and there is no separate military fab, so slowing the national compute base slows military programs. CON's core defense—that military AI runs on mature nodes and narrow models—is a legitimate line but was repeatedly asserted rather than developed, and its "emergency is industrial, not military" answer was effectively absorbed by PRO's "grant it fully, same compute pool" move. CON's strongest point (lost volume taxes the lead's own next tool generation) was real but undercut when CON conceded it could name no delayed tool generation and fell back to "record books can hide a hole." Both sides misreferenced IDs in pressure questions (C/P prefixes), roughly cancelling. CON was competent and coherent but left PRO's weighing largely intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1/A2 in Rebuttal 2: conceding that no fielded system this decade needs new wafers, then flipping the question—"a fielded system is, by definition, already trained"—and showing "months" is a per-cycle penalty that compounds across a decade, while pinning CON to treating the same constraint as trivial for the adversary and existential for toolmakers.</best_rebuttal>
